newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan civilians suffer in artillery duel for Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan civilians suffer in artillery duel for Kabul.

text.p: Ousted Afghan government forces fought rocket and artillery duels with the Taleban militia on Wednesday over the important De Sabz pass just 10 km (6 miles) north of the Afghan capital Kabul.

Shell after shell and salvoes of rockets fired by troops of the mainly Tajik Jamiat-i-Islami faction under the leadership of deposed government commander Ahmad Shah Masood slammed into positions around the pass held by the the radical Islamic Taleban militia.

Masood, famed leader of Afghan guerrillas in their war against Soviet occupation in the early 1980s, is trying to dislodge Taleban forces from Kabul which the fundamentalist militia force captured a month ago.
The road from Masood-controlled territory into northeast Kabul cuts through the pass and would give government forces command over heights vital to an advance on the capital.

Jamiat commanders in the village of Kalakan, around 20km (12 miles) north of Kabul, said government forces opened up an artillery barrage at 4 a.m. (00.30 GMT) and sent in troops to encircle Taleban troops on the De Sabz pass.
"We're moving round to encircle them and we will move on Kabul, God willing," said Abdul Rahim Yusufi, a field commander clutching a walkie-talkie.
Some of his 300 men in Kalakan looked tired after the previous day's festive atmosphere in anticipation of the offensive.
"We control the hills around the pass but we have not yet taken the road," Mehrabodin Masstan, a spokesman for Masood, told reporters.
Despite an immense display of fire power, including troops, artillery and rocket batteries belonging to the northern Uzbek leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, Taleban troops put up tough resistance.
A second pass, Khair Khana, which straddles the main road into Kabul, also remains in the hands of the Taleban.

Mohammed Suhail, 40, watched the rockets' blazing arcs and explosions on the barren hills around the pass from the roof of his house in the village of Bagram, 35 km (25 miles) north of Kabul. Tomatoes and yellow corn cobs were drying in the sun on an adjacent roof.
"We have to resist the Taleban as we resisted the Russians," he said, referring to the 10-year war against the Soviets. "It is better to fight than be killed by the Taleban."
His eight children darted around the house's mud-walled garden of vines and fruit trees.
One of them, 13-year-old Mobares, said: "I can't go to school. We just sit at home and watch the fighting all day."
Tens of thousands of Afghans have been killed in the bitter faction-fighting which has torn apart the mountainous country of 17 million.
In a grubby, run-down hospital in Charikar, a small town 45 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, one-year-old Mariam lay unconcious next to her older brother Ezad, aged 5.
Both were badly wounded, she in the head and he in the back.

Their father, Mehrabuddin (one name), said a Taleban warplane dropped a cluster bomb on his home in Kalakan on Wednesday where his children had been playing. He said their mother was killed in the attack.
Mehrabuddin made no other comment. But when bystanders expressed their condolences, a man next to him said simply: "That is war."
